notes: Trigger cases only. The skill is installed for every case in this file; the
question is whether it fires, not whether it exists. should_trigger cases
measure recall, should_not_trigger cases measure precision.
The should_not_trigger set is the part that earns its keep. Every entry is a
near-miss chosen to be genuinely adjacent -- git branch work, parallel work,
isolation, cleanup -- so a description that over-claims fires on them. Cases
that obviously belong to another domain prove nothing, and a corpus full of
those reports a precision the skill has not earned.
should_trigger: I need to work on two branches at once without stashing. Set that up.
Create an isolated workspace for this feature so I don't disturb my current checkout.
Set up a git worktree for the refactor branch.
I'm about to start executing an implementation plan and want it isolated from main.
Show me the worktrees on this repo and remove the ones I've already merged.
The feature is done in the worktree -- merge it back to main and clean up.
Where should I put a new worktree so git doesn't try to track it?
I have three stale worktrees and their branches left over. Tear them down.
should_not_trigger: Create a new branch called feature/login and switch to it.
I have uncommitted changes I need to set aside for a minute.
Run the test suite on this branch and tell me what fails.
Merge main into my current branch and resolve the conflicts.
Delete the local branches that have already been merged.
Clone this repository into a second directory so I can compare versions.
